title: Worked journey: One dataset, end to end

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
An end-to-end analysis takes one question from raw data to its final table and figure in a single script that another person can run.

The analysis is reproducible in this book’s sense when the outputs come back the same from the raw files with that one command.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Eight steps, in the order real work runs them.

  1. The question. One sentence, saying who, what is measured, and how it is summarised.
  2. The data. Download the raw files. Read the terms that come with them. Record each file’s checksum.
  3. The dictionary. One row per variable you will use: its name in the file, its meaning, its unit, its codes, and where you found them.
  4. The project folder. data-raw/ for the files as they arrived, code/ for the script, output/ for what the script makes.
  5. The script. Read, check, join, clean, work out new columns, summarise, plot, write the outputs, print the versions.
  6. The README. What the project is, where the data came from, and the one command that reruns it.
  7. The rerun. Delete the outputs and run the command from nothing. The same table and the same figure must come back.
  8. What it does not show. Say it, next to the result.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with the question, written in one sentence before you touch the data:

Among adults aged 20 and over who were examined in NHANES between August 2021 and August 2023 and were not pregnant at the exam, how is measured body mass index (BMI) spread in men and in women?

BMI is weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres, measured in kg/m2. The question names who (adults examined in one survey cycle, not pregnant), what is measured (BMI from measured weight and height), and how it is summarised (its spread, by gender). It does not ask about the United States. That matters later.

Now the data. NHANES, the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, publishes each part of the survey as its own file. The measurements are in the body measures file, BMX_L. Age, gender and pregnancy are in the demographics file, DEMO_L. Both carry SEQN, the respondent sequence number, which is the key that joins them. You download both .xpt files from the survey’s website and put them, unchanged, in data-raw/.

Before using them, read the terms. NHANES files come under the Data User Agreement of the National Center for Health Statistics, the American agency that runs the survey. Among other things, users agree to “Use the data in this dataset for statistical reporting and analysis only” and to “Make no attempt to learn the identity of any person or establishment included in these data”. Neither the agreement nor the documentation states a copyright licence. Write the terms in the README.

Then record what arrived. Take each file’s MD5 checksum, as in the section on reading raw files, and count its rows:

library(haven)
library(here)

unname(tools::md5sum(here("data-raw", c("BMX_L.xpt", "DEMO_L.xpt"))))

bmx <- read_xpt(here("data-raw", "BMX_L.xpt"))
demo <- read_xpt(here("data-raw", "DEMO_L.xpt"))
nrow(bmx)
nrow(demo)
here() starts at ~/project
[1] "ab25a36296e5b61881d42fef61c06b84"
[2] "14555b1f4e3c909172e900f63a2ecd03"
[1] 8860
[1] 11933

The body measures file has 8860 rows, one for each person examined. The demographics file has 11933, because it also holds people who were interviewed and never examined. The two checksums go in the README, so that anyone can confirm later that they have the same files.

Next, the dictionary. Write it from the survey’s own documentation, the codebook pages for the two files, for the variables the question needs and no others:

Variable Meaning, with unit Codes Source
SEQN respondent sequence number, one per person a number both codebooks; checked unique in the file
RIAGENDR gender 1 Male, 2 Female DEMO_L codebook
RIDAGEYR age in years at the screening interview 0 to 79; 80 means 80 and over DEMO_L codebook
RIDEXPRG pregnancy status at the exam 1 pregnant, 2 not pregnant, 3 cannot tell; missing for anyone not asked DEMO_L codebook
BMXWT weight, kg measured value BMX_L codebook
BMXHT standing height, cm measured value BMX_L codebook
BMXBMI BMI, kg/m2, worked out from weight and height and rounded to one decimal worked-out value BMX_L codebook

Two entries will matter in the script. Ages of 80 and over are all written as 80, so no age in the file is above 80. And the pregnancy question was asked only of some women, so the column is missing for every man and for most women. Type the dictionary once, by hand, and save it as data-raw/nhanes_dictionary.csv beside the raw files.

The project folder is the one this book has used throughout: data-raw/, code/ and output/. The README goes at the top. Write it now, with the outputs named, and treat its rerun line as a promise you are about to test:

BMI of adults in NHANES 2021–2023, by gender

The spread of measured BMI in men and women aged 20 and over, not pregnant at the exam, examined in NHANES August 2021–August 2023. Every summary is unweighted and describes these participants only.

Raw data: data-raw/BMX_L.xpt (MD5 ab25a36296e5b61881d42fef61c06b84) and data-raw/DEMO_L.xpt (MD5 14555b1f4e3c909172e900f63a2ecd03), downloaded unchanged from the NHANES website. Use is governed by the NCHS Data User Agreement: statistical reporting and analysis only, and no attempt to identify anyone.

Data dictionary: data-raw/nhanes_dictionary.csv.

To rerun: open a terminal in this folder and type Rscript code/analysis.R. The script reads data-raw/, never writes to it, and writes output/bmi_by_gender.csv (the table) and output/bmi_by_gender.png (the figure).

Written with R 4.3.3; the versions of every package are printed at the end of each run. Contact: your name and email address.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
These files came with complete documentation, a stated key and published terms. A thesis dataset exported from a form tool, or a register typed up from a clinic, often comes with none of the three. Then the dictionary is written from the questionnaire and from asking the people who collected the data, and the README says so.

The checksums prove that your files are the files you recorded. They cannot prove that those are the files the survey published, unless the survey also publishes checksums.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Build the script a step at a time, checking the row count after each step. One step goes wrong.

Join the demographics onto the body measures by SEQN, as in the section on joining. A left_join() keeps every row of the left table, so the count must stay at 8860. relationship = "one-to-one" tells the join to stop with an error if a key turns up twice in either file:

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

n_distinct(bmx$SEQN)
n_distinct(demo$SEQN)

nhanes <- bmx |>
  left_join(demo, by = "SEQN", relationship = "one-to-one")
nrow(nhanes)
[1] 8860
[1] 11933
[1] 8860

Each file has as many distinct SEQN values as rows, so the key is one per person in both. The join added no row and lost none. Now keep the adults:

adults <- nhanes |>
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20)
nrow(adults)

adults |>
  count(RIDEXPRG)
[1] 6064
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  RIDEXPRG     n
     <dbl> <int>
1        1    41
2        2  1065
3        3    28
4       NA  4930

6064 adults. Of them, 41 were pregnant at the exam (code 1). The question leaves them out, so you expect 6064 minus 41, which is 6023 rows, after the next step. Here is the first draft of that line:

first_try <- adults |>
  filter(RIDEXPRG != 1)
nrow(first_try)
[1] 1093

1093, not 6023. The line meant to drop 41 people dropped 4971. The reason is the 4930 rows where RIDEXPRG is missing: every man, and every woman who was not asked. For them RIDEXPRG != 1 is neither true nor false. It is NA, and filter() keeps only the rows where the test is TRUE. The line ran without a warning and gave a plausible table of 1093 adults. All of them were women whose pregnancy status was recorded as code 2 or 3, and no man was left. Only the expected count caught it.

Say what you mean instead: keep a row if the value is missing, or if it is not 1.

adults <- adults |>
  filter(is.na(RIDEXPRG) | RIDEXPRG != 1)
nrow(adults)
sum(!is.na(adults$BMXBMI))
[1] 6023
[1] 5929

6023, as expected. Of these, 5929 have a BMI; the other 94 lack a weight or a height.

One more check before trusting the BMI column. The codebook says BMI was worked out as weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared, then rounded to one decimal. Work it out again and find the largest gap between yours and the file’s. abs() drops the sign of a difference.

bmi_check <- adults$BMXWT / (adults$BMXHT / 100)^2
max(abs(bmi_check - adults$BMXBMI), na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 0.04996478

The largest gap is under 0.05 kg/m2, which is what rounding to one decimal allows. So the column is what the codebook says it is.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The expected count caught the pregnancy filter because count() gave the number of pregnant adults before the filter (41, the codebook’s figure too), so you knew what to expect. A filter whose correct result you cannot predict has no such check. Count the rows it removes, and look at a few of them.

The BMI check compares the file with itself. It confirms the column was worked out as documented. It cannot catch a weight or height that was measured or recorded wrongly.

blocks.label: Illustration 3
blocks.html:
Now put the steps that survived into the script, in order, with a comment for each. This is the whole of code/analysis.R:

# analysis.R
# BMI of adults aged 20 and over, by gender, in NHANES August
# 2021-August 2023 (files BMX_L and DEMO_L), leaving out anyone
# pregnant at the exam.
# Run from the project folder: Rscript code/analysis.R
# Reads data-raw/ and never writes to it; writes two files to
# output/. Every summary is unweighted: it describes these
# participants only.

library(haven)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)

dir.create(here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)

# 1. Read the two raw files
bmx <- read_xpt(here("data-raw", "BMX_L.xpt"))
demo <- read_xpt(here("data-raw", "DEMO_L.xpt"))
cat("Participants with body measures:", nrow(bmx), "\n")

# 2. Check the key: one row per participant in each file
stopifnot(
  "SEQN is unique in BMX_L" = n_distinct(bmx$SEQN) == nrow(bmx),
  "SEQN is unique in DEMO_L" = n_distinct(demo$SEQN) == nrow(demo)
)

# 3. Join demographics onto body measures; no row added or lost
nhanes <- bmx |>
  left_join(demo, by = "SEQN", relationship = "one-to-one")
stopifnot("the join kept every row" = nrow(nhanes) == nrow(bmx))

# 4. Keep adults not pregnant at the exam. RIDEXPRG is missing
#    for everyone not asked, so missing rows are kept on purpose.
adults <- nhanes |>
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20) |>
  filter(is.na(RIDEXPRG) | RIDEXPRG != 1) |>
  mutate(
    gender = factor(RIAGENDR, levels = c(1, 2),
                    labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    bmi_check = BMXWT / (BMXHT / 100)^2
  ) |>
  select(SEQN, gender, age = RIDAGEYR, weight_kg = BMXWT,
         height_cm = BMXHT, bmi = BMXBMI, bmi_check)
cat("Adults kept:", nrow(adults), "\n")
cat("Adults with a BMI:", sum(!is.na(adults$bmi)), "\n")

# 5. Check the values. Limits set before looking at the data;
#    a value outside them stops the script so that you look.
stopifnot(
  "measured adult heights are between 50 and 250 cm" =
    all(adults$height_cm >= 50 & adults$height_cm <= 250,
        na.rm = TRUE),
  "measured adult weights are between 20 and 300 kg" =
    all(adults$weight_kg >= 20 & adults$weight_kg <= 300,
        na.rm = TRUE),
  "BMI agrees with weight / height^2 to rounding" =
    all(abs(adults$bmi - adults$bmi_check) <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
)

# 6. Summarise BMI by gender, with the n behind every number.
#    The mean is rounded for display, to BMI's one decimal.
bmi_by_gender <- adults |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarise(
    n_adults = n(),
    n_bmi = sum(!is.na(bmi)),
    mean_bmi = round(mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    q1_bmi = quantile(bmi, probs = 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_bmi = median(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
    q3_bmi = quantile(bmi, probs = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
print(bmi_by_gender)
write_csv(bmi_by_gender, here("output", "bmi_by_gender.csv"))

# 7. Plot the spread of BMI by gender
bmi_plot <- adults |>
  filter(!is.na(bmi)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gender, y = bmi)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "BMI (kg/m^2)",
    caption = "NHANES 2021-2023, aged 20+, not pregnant; unweighted"
  )
ggsave(here("output", "bmi_by_gender.png"), plot = bmi_plot,
       width = 5, height = 4, units = "in", dpi = 150)

# 8. Record the versions that made these outputs
sessionInfo()

Read it from the top and you can name the section of this book behind each step: the project folder and here(), reading a raw file, checks that stop the script, the join, choosing rows, new columns and factors, summaries by group, the plot, and the fresh run. cat() prints its arguments as one line of text, which gives the run a short log of counts, and "\n" ends the line. In step 4, labels = gives the names that replace the codes, in the order of levels. In step 7, the pipe hands the data to ggplot(); the layers after it still join with +. NULL leaves that axis without a title. dpi sets the dots per inch, the image’s sharpness.

Read the table as the dictionary and the question tell you to. There are 2680 men and 3249 women with a BMI, and 2680 + 3249 = 5929, the count in the log. Every check passed, or the script would have stopped at it. The versions printed below the table are the record of what produced it.

The three quartiles answer the question, as R’s default (type 7) gives them: a quarter of the values lie below the first quartile, half below the median, three quarters below the third quartile.

The median BMI is 28.1 kg/m2 in men and 28.7 kg/m2 in women (unweighted: these participants only), close together. The spread is not. The middle half of the women runs from 24.4 to 34.7 kg/m2, a width of 10.3 kg/m2. The middle half of the men runs from 24.9 to 32.4 kg/m2, a width of 7.5 kg/m2. The women’s upper quarter reaches higher. The means, 29.3 and 30.3 kg/m2, sit above both medians, because a long tail of high values pulls a mean up and leaves a median where it is.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The range limits in step 5 are the ones the section on checks used, and they are wide on purpose: they stop the script for a height of 17 cm or a weight of 700 kg, not for an unusual but real adult. They passed here partly because the survey’s own team had already reviewed the values. Their documentation says values judged unrealistic “were deleted from the file”. A file nobody has reviewed may stop at step 5, and that is the step doing its job.

The script handles these two files. If the survey releases a corrected file, its checksum will differ from the README’s, and the counts in the log may change. Rerun, compare, and record the new checksum.

blocks.label: Illustration 4
blocks.html:
The rerun is the test the whole book has been building to. Start from nothing: delete output/, run the command again, and compare the new table with the old one, byte for byte.

cp output/bmi_by_gender.csv first_run.csv
rm -r output
Rscript code/analysis.R > /dev/null 2>&1
ls output
cmp first_run.csv output/bmi_by_gender.csv && echo "identical"
cat output/bmi_by_gender.csv
bmi_by_gender.csv
bmi_by_gender.png
identical
gender,n_adults,n_bmi,mean_bmi,q1_bmi,median_bmi,q3_bmi
Male,2720,2680,29.3,24.9,28.1,32.4
Female,3303,3249,30.3,24.4,28.7,34.7

cp copies a file and rm -r deletes a folder. > /dev/null 2>&1 throws away what the run prints. cmp compares two files and prints nothing when they are the same. && runs the next command only if the last one succeeded, and echo prints its words.

Both outputs came back, and the table is identical to the one before. A colleague with the project folder runs the same command on their computer. If their table differs, the checksums and the version lines are where the two of you start looking. This is the gate to the next rung, the test you must pass before moving on to it: the analysis reproduces from the raw data with one command.

Now say what it does not show, in the README and next to any number you quote from it.

  • It does not estimate anything about the United States. The survey’s documentation says its sample weights “should be used to analyze the body measures data”. This analysis uses none, so its summaries describe these 5929 participants and nobody else. Weights are taught in the subject on India’s data infrastructure and complex surveys.
  • It says nothing about India, or about adults anywhere else.
  • BMI is worked out from weight and height. It is not a measurement of body fat.
  • It is one examination of each person. It says nothing about change over time, or about what causes a higher or lower BMI.
  • Its correctness rests on the checks. A mistake that passes every check reruns perfectly.

The next rung of this subject takes the same project further. A block of code repeated three times becomes a function you write, and you run it over many columns, files or groups at once. Git records every change to the script. A Quarto document replaces the step where you copy 28.1 into your text: the code writes the number into the document itself. DuckDB queries files too big to read into R at once. A form tool such as KoboToolbox, ODK or REDCap writes the raw file at the point where the data are collected.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The rerun on one computer shows the script is complete. It does not show that a computer with other package versions gets the same table; only a second person’s run shows that, and pinning the versions is two rungs up.

The comparison here is of the CSV file. Compare a figure by looking at it: an image file can differ in its bytes when nothing you would see has changed.

points.html: Write the question before you open the data, and write who it is about.
The error is to trust a filter because it ran without a warning. Before each filter, write down how many rows you expect it to keep, and check.
Record each raw file’s checksum in the README on the day it arrives, and the terms it came with.
Put a printed row count after every step that can add or drop rows, and a stopifnot() where you know the right count.

Any summary of an NHANES file without its sample weights describes the participants in the file. Write “unweighted” beside it, and never present it as the figure for the United States, still less for India.
The gate is one command from raw data to the same outputs. Ask for it before you read a single result.
Reproducible means the result can be checked, not that it is right. A wrong cut-point or a wrong filter reruns perfectly.

blocks.label: Common misreading
blocks.html: “NHANES shows the median BMI of American women is 28.7 kg/m2.” The table does not say that. It gives the median of 3249 women examined in one survey cycle. It uses none of the survey’s sample weights, and the survey’s documentation says those weights should be used. So 28.7 kg/m2 describes these participants. Read it as “in this sample”, never as “in America”.

blocks.prompt: Without looking back, list the steps of an end-to-end analysis in the order real work runs them. Then say what the gate to the next rung is.
blocks.answer:
The steps, in order:

  1. The question.
  2. The raw files, their terms and their checksums.
  3. The data dictionary.
  4. The project folder.
  5. The script. It reads, checks, joins, cleans, works out new columns, summarises, plots, writes its outputs and prints the versions.
  6. The README, with the one command.
  7. A rerun from nothing.
  8. What the result does not show.

The gate: the analysis reproduces from the raw data with one command, Rscript code/analysis.R, in a fresh session.

blocks.prompt:
Build the rung’s target with a dataset of your own. It may be a thesis dataset, or a department register you have permission to use. It may be the NHANES files of this section, with a question of your own.

Write the question in one sentence. Put the raw files in data-raw/ and record their checksums and terms. Write the data dictionary.

Write code/analysis.R so that it reads, checks, cleans, summarises and plots, writes one table and one figure to output/, and ends with sessionInfo(). Write the README. Then delete output/, run Rscript code/analysis.R in a fresh session, and give the project folder to a colleague to run the same command.
blocks.answer:
The project passes when all of these hold.

  1. The question is one sentence and says who the answer is about.
  2. data-raw/ holds the files exactly as they arrived. Their checksums in the README match tools::md5sum() on them now. No code writes to that folder.
  3. The dictionary has a row for every variable the script uses. Each row gives the name exactly as in the file, its meaning, unit and codes, and where each came from.
  4. The script reads every file with here(). It needs no object, package or file that it does not load or make itself.
  5. It prints the row count after each step that can add or drop rows. It stops with stopifnot() where a count, a key or a range is wrong.
  6. Every change to the data is a line of code with a comment. No cell was edited by hand.
  7. Every summary prints its n. A survey summary says whether it is weighted.
  8. The table and the figure are written to output/ by code, and the script ends with sessionInfo().
  9. After output/ is deleted, Rscript code/analysis.R brings back the same table, byte for byte.
  10. Your colleague’s run gives the same table. If it does not, the two sessionInfo() printouts are compared and the difference is written in the README.

Write, beside the result, what it does not show.

blocks.prompt: A colleague sends you the project for her thesis chapter. The README says: “Run the scripts in code/ in order.” code/ holds clean.R and analysis.R. The first line of clean.R is data <- read_excel("C:/Users/anita/Desktop/final data (2).xlsx"). Its last line is write_xlsx(data, "C:/Users/anita/Desktop/final data (2).xlsx"). Her chapter reports “mean BMI 24.6 kg/m2 (n = 412)”. Find each thing that stops this project from passing the gate, and say what each one would cost her.
blocks.answer:
Five things stop it from passing.

  • The README gives no single command, and “in order” leaves the reader guessing. Fix: one script, or one command that runs both, written in the README.
  • The path is absolute and names her desktop, so the script stops on every other computer. Fix: put the file in data-raw/ and read it with here().
  • The last line writes over the file it read. After one run the raw data are gone, replaced by the cleaned version, and nothing can be rerun from the original. Fix: never write to the raw file; write cleaned data to output/ if it is needed at all.
  • The file name “final data (2)” says there was a “final data (1)”. Nobody can tell which one the chapter used. Fix: record the raw file’s checksum in the README.
  • The number 24.6 kg/m2 has no line of code that writes it to a file, so it was copied off a screen. Fix: write the table to output/ with code and take the number from there.

The cost: as it stands, nobody, including Anita in a year, can show that 24.6 kg/m2 comes from the data collected. Her examiner can ask, and she cannot answer.

blocks.prompt: A health secretary asks why the department’s analysts should hand over every analysis as a project folder that reruns with one command. Answer on one page. Put the answer first, then the reasons, with no methods section.
blocks.answer:
Answer: because then someone else can check any number in a departmental report in minutes. Without it, nobody can check it at all.

  • Mistakes are found before publication, not after. A rerun by a second analyst catches a step that lived only on one laptop.
  • Work survives people. When an analyst leaves, the next one reruns the folder instead of starting again.
  • Corrections are cheap. When the raw data are corrected, the same command remakes every table.
  • The cost is small. It is a habit and free software, not a purchase.

What it does not buy: a rerunnable analysis can still ask the wrong question. Someone still has to read it.
